title: Medieval manuscripts are "biological time capsules" for deadly sheeppox virus
gist: Researchers extracted and sequenced sheeppox virus DNA preserved in the animal-skin parchment of medieval manuscripts, reconstructing 3,500 years of the virus's evolution and showing that historical archives worldwide may hold hidden genetic records of past livestock disease outbreaks.

themes.theme: A new method for reading disease history from parchment

insights.claim: Scientists extracted and sequenced sheeppox virus DNA preserved in the animal-skin parchment of medieval manuscripts to reconstruct how the virus evolved over roughly 3,500 years.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Establishes parchment as a viable, previously untapped biological archive for studying historical animal pathogens.
insights.locator: In order to reconstruct how the virus has evolved

insights.claim: Co-author Louis L’Hôte said archives and libraries around the world may contain genetic traces of past animal disease outbreaks preserved in parchment, since ancient pathogen DNA research has already transformed understanding of historic infectious disease.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Suggests a large, largely unexplored global research opportunity in existing manuscript collections for tracking historical disease evolution.
insights.quote: It is possible that archives and libraries around the world also contain the genetic traces of disease outbreaks in animals in the past
insights.locator: "The recording of ancient DNA of pathogens has completely changed our understanding

themes.theme: A long written and genetic record of outbreaks

insights.claim: The earliest known written evidence of sheeppox dates to first-century CE Roman accounts of skin lesions in sheep, with more frequent references to deadly outbreaks recorded in medieval agricultural and accounting texts across France, Spain, and England.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Provides a documentary baseline against which the new genetic findings can be cross-checked.
insights.locator: Per the authors, the earliest known written evidence

insights.claim: Sheeppox outbreaks declined in 17th-century France but resurged with high mortality in the 18th and 19th centuries, while Great Britain did not experience a resurgence until 1847.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Documents a centuries-long boom-bust pattern in outbreak intensity that the genomic data can now help explain.
insights.locator: There seemed to be a decline in outbreaks in 17th-century France

insights.claim: The research team sampled manuscripts held at Yale University, Cambridge University, Corpus Christi College, University College Dublin, the Lambeth Palace Library, and Trinity College, and found sheeppox DNA on multiple pages of the same manuscripts, indicating medieval flocks experienced frequent outbreaks.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Confirms sheeppox was widespread enough in medieval flocks to leave a detectable genetic signature across multiple independent manuscript collections.
insights.locator: Multiple pages, often from the same manuscript

insights.claim: Researchers were surprised to also find sheeppox virus DNA on parchment made from calfskin and goatskin, suggesting either cross-species infection or contamination during parchment manufacturing.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: An unexpected finding that complicates the simple assumption that parchment DNA always matches the animal species it was made from.
insights.locator: The authors were surprised when they also found evidence

themes.theme: Reconstructing the virus's deep evolutionary timeline

insights.claim: By comparing medieval genomes with DNA from Bronze Age sheep teeth found at settlement sites in Russia and Central Kazakhstan, researchers concluded sheeppox diverged from the goatpox and lumpy skin disease viruses between 11,500 and 3,700 years ago, roughly coinciding with animal domestication in Europe.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Links a specific viral divergence event to the broader historical process of animal domestication, a new data point for veterinary evolutionary biology.
insights.locator: the authors concluded that the sheeppox virus diverged

insights.claim: The team recovered 21 ancient sheeppox genomes spanning from 1700 BCE to early modern Europe.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of the new genomic dataset now available for future research on livestock pathogen evolution.
insights.locator: All told, the team recovered 21 ancient genomes

insights.claim: Co-author Kevin G. Daly said the project shows that parchment—long considered a vanishing craft—preserves not just cultural history but the historical landscape of livestock disease, achievable only through interdisciplinary collaboration.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Frames the discovery as a template for future interdisciplinary science combining historical archives with modern genomics.
insights.quote: This project shows that parchments not only preserve our cultural history for hundreds of years, but also the landscape of disease in our livestock in the medieval period.
insights.locator: "Parchment making has been considered a vanishing craft
